title: The Accent-Stripping One-Liner Broke Our Search Results in Korean
partialText:
Stack Overflow’s top accent fix changes string length, so for three months we cut Korean snippets in the wrong place.

In July we made our search accent-insensitive. Type “skoda” and you find “Škoda”. Type “cafe” and you find “café”. It took one line, the same line most JavaScript developers reach for, and it fixed search for every user writing in French, Czech, Polish or Vietnamese.

For the next three months, that line also meant a Korean user searching their chat history got results whose preview did not contain the word they searched for. Sometimes the preview was just “…”. The search was right. The preview was cut in the wrong place.

I co-founded AI Toolbox, a Chrome extension used by 40,000 people that adds full-text search to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok. Each search result shows a snippet: a short window of the message with your word in the middle. This is the story of how a famous one-liner broke that window for Korean and Japanese text, why our tests never noticed, and the small change that fixed it.

The One-Liner Everyone Copies

The Stack Overflow question “Remove accents/diacritics in a string in JavaScript” had been viewed 592,224 times as of October 2026. Its top answer, at a score of 2,101, is this:

const str = "Crème Brûlée"
str.normalize("NFD").replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, "")
> "Creme Brulee"

normalize("NFD") splits a precomposed letter into a base letter plus a combining mark, so "è" becomes "e" followed by U+0300. The regular expression then deletes every mark in the range U+0300 to U+036F. Our version lowercased first and mapped a few atomic letters such as "ł" and "ø", and we ran it on both the query and the text, so "skoda" and "Škoda" both became "skoda".

The answer is correct for what it was asked: comparing strings. The bug came from what we did next. To build a snippet, we found the match in the folded text and then cut the original text at the same position. Our own comment said why that was safe:

“the folded string keeps the SAME length and the SAME character offsets as the lowercased original. That length-preservation is deliberately relied on by the snippet/highlight code”

And it said why other scripts were not at risk:

“Non-Latin scripts (CJK, Arabic, Hebrew, Cyrillic) carry no combining marks to strip and pass through unchanged”

Both sentences were wrong. Here is the snippet code from our Gemini module, as it shipped in July:

export function getContextSnippet(content: string, query: string, contextChars: number = 58): string {
  // Accent-folded, length-preserving lookup: an accent-insensitive query still
  // centres the snippet on the match, and the offset is valid on the original.
  const matchIndex = foldAccents(content).indexOf(foldAccents(query));
  if (matchIndex === -1) return content.substring(0, contextChars * 2);
  const start = Math.max(0, matchIndex - contextChars);
  const end = Math.min(content.length, matchIndex + query.length + contextChars);
  let snippet = content.substring(start, end);

matchIndex comes from one string. content.substring cuts another. The ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and cross-app search modules each had their own copy of the same pattern, five in all.

What NFD Actually Does to Korean

NFD does not only split accented Latin letters. It decomposes anything that has a canonical decomposition, and the regular expression only removes marks in one block.

Every Korean syllable decomposes. “한” becomes three jamo, U+1112 U+1161 U+11AB. “가” becomes two. The Unicode normalization report, UAX #15, notes that “the decompositions and compositions for Hangul syllables are algorithmic”: a syllable splits into two jamo, or three when it has a final consonant. None of those jamo are in U+0300 to U+036F, so the regular expression keeps all of them.

Japanese voiced kana do the same thing. “が” becomes “か” plus U+3099, and “パ” becomes “ハ” plus U+309A. Arabic alef with madda, “آ”, becomes alef plus U+0653. Even MDN’s page on normalize() states it plainly: the NFD form of "ñ" has a length of 2.

So folding is not length-preserving at all for Korean. “한국어” is 3 characters and folds to 8. In the sentence “결론적으로 데이터베이스”, the word “데이터베이스” sits at position 6 in the original and at position 14 in the folded text, and the whole sentence grows from 12 characters to 26.

One more claim in that comment was off. Cyrillic does not pass through unchanged: “й” decomposes to “и” plus U+0306, so it folds to “и”, and “ё” folds to “е”. Searching Russian is still accent-insensitive in the way Russian readers expect for “ё”, so we kept that behavior and corrected the comment.

Three Months of Previews That Missed the Word

Feed a position from the folded text into the original, and the snippet window lands two to three times too far along a Korean message, because every syllable before the match counts as two or three.

I ran the July code against a Korean message with “데이터베이스” in the middle. The word starts at position 138; the folded text put it at 274, so the window it returned was a stretch of the message well after the word, and the preview never showed it. With the word near the end of a message, the computed start fell past the end of the text, substring returned an empty string, and the preview was just "...". Japanese text drifted by one position for every voiced kana before the match, so its previews were off-centre rather than empty.

Nothing else looked wrong, which is why it lasted. Matching folded both sides the same way, so Korean searches found the right messages. Our tests checked matching and highlighting, and none of them sliced Korean text. Before July 23 every snippet builder used toLowerCase().indexOf(), which keeps the length for these scripts, so the bug arrived in the same commit that made search accent-insensitive.

The Second Bug Hiding Next to It: \b

Exact Match, a Premium option in our Advanced search, matches whole words only, and JavaScript’s word boundary does not know what a word is outside English.

MDN’s word boundary page defines a word character as a letter from A to Z or a to z, a digit from 0 to 9, or an underscore. So /\bкот\b/.test("мой кот спит") returns false. A Korean, Cyrillic, Greek or Arabic term has no boundary for \b to find.

Our search already knew this. One helper adds \b only on a side where the term starts or ends with an ASCII word character, and otherwise falls back to a substring match:

export function exactWordPattern(term: string): string {
  const lead = /^\w/.test(term) ? "\\b" : "";
  const trail = /\w$/.test(term) ? "\\b" : "";
  return `${lead}${escapeRegExp(term)}${trail}`;
}

But the snippet builders in the ChatGPT and Claude modules, and the highlighter shared by all four, built their own \b...\b patterns. With Exact Match on, search found the Russian message and then the preview code could not find the word in it. In ChatGPT and Claude the result showed the whole message with nothing highlighted; in Gemini and Grok the window was right but the word was not highlighted. The fix was to use the same rule in all three places, so a term cannot match in search and then fail to match in its own preview.

The Fix: Return a Map, Not an Offset

Any transform that can change a string’s length has to give you a way back to the original. Ours now does, in one shared function that all five snippet builders call:

export function locateFolded(original: string, query: string | RegExp): FoldedMatch | null {
  if (!original) return null;
  const folded = foldAccents(original);
  let at = -1;
  let len = 0;
  if (typeof query === "string") {
    const needle = foldAccents(query);
    if (!needle) return null;
    at = folded.indexOf(needle);
    len = needle.length;
  } else {
    const hit = new RegExp(query.source, query.flags.replace("g", "")).exec(folded);
    if (hit) {
      at = hit.index;
      len = hit[0].length;
    }
  }
  if (at < 0 || len === 0) return null;
  if (folded.length === original.length && !HAS_MARK.test(original)) {
    return { index: at, length: len };
  }
  const stop = at + len;
  let pos = 0;
  let index = -1;
  for (const m of original.matchAll(CLUSTER)) {
    const start = m.index ?? 0;
    const next = pos + foldedLength(m[0]);
    if (index < 0 && next > at) index = start;
    if (next >= stop) return { index, length: start + m[0].length - index };
    pos = next;
  }
  return null;
}

Matching itself barely changed. It still folds the whole string once and calls indexOf; the only difference is Greek final sigma, below. What changed is that a match is translated back into the original before anything is sliced. Three details carry the weight.

It walks clusters, not characters. CLUSTER is /\P{M}\p{M}*|\p{M}+/gu: a base character plus the marks after it. NFD only reorders marks inside such a cluster, so folding cluster by cluster gives exactly the same string as folding the whole text. The one context-sensitive lowercase rule in JavaScript, Greek final sigma, would break that, so we now fold "ς" to "σ" as well.

It skips the walk when it can prove nothing moved. Folding only ever deletes combining marks. If the original has none, every character folds to at least its own length, so if the total length is unchanged, every character folded to exactly its own length and the offsets are already correct. That covers nearly all English and European text.

It counts Korean syllables with arithmetic. Korean text cannot take the shortcut, so foldedLength computes a syllable's folded length directly, two jamo or three, instead of normalizing it. A test checks that shortcut against normalize for all 11,172 Hangul syllables.

The first version of the fix walked every cluster of every message and took 29ms on a 100,000 character English message, against 0.6ms for the old code. With the shortcut it takes 1.1ms. A 100,000 character Korean message with the match at the very end, the worst case, takes 9.8ms. Real messages are far shorter, and the snippet runs once per visible result.

The Korean message whose preview missed the word now shows the sentence it sits in, 결론적으로 데이터베이스 마이그레이션은 미루기로 했습니다, with the word in the middle.

What I Would Tell Anyone Copying That Answer

The Stack Overflow answer is fine. It answers “make these two strings compare equal”, and for that it works. The bug is using its output as a coordinate system.

  • If you only compare, you may not need to fold at all. new Intl.Collator(undefined, { sensitivity: "base" }).compare("cafe", "Café") returns 0, with no string changed. It cannot find a substring position, which is why search code folds instead.
  • If you fold and need positions, keep a map back. Any offset found in a transformed string belongs to that string only.
  • Test the scripts your users write in, not the ones you write in. One Korean sentence and one Japanese sentence in the snippet tests would have caught this in July.
  • A comment that states an invariant needs a test that checks it. Ours said “length-preservation is deliberately relied on” in capital letters, and no test checked the length.

Key Takeaways

  • normalize("NFD") changes string length for far more than accented Latin letters: every Korean syllable, Japanese voiced kana, and some Arabic letters.
  • An offset found in a folded or normalized string is not an offset in the original. Map it back before you slice.
  • JavaScript’s \b only recognizes the letters A to Z and a to z, the digits 0 to 9, and underscore, so whole-word patterns built from it never match Korean, Cyrillic, Greek or Arabic terms.
  • Search, snippet and highlight code should share one matching rule. When they disagree, the result list contradicts itself.
  • A fast path that proves offsets are unchanged keeps the fix nearly free for Latin text.

FAQ

Does normalize("NFD") change a string's length? Yes. NFD splits precomposed characters into a base plus combining marks, so "ñ" goes from length 1 to 2. Stripping U+0300 to U+036F restores the length only for accented Latin letters. Korean syllables become two or three jamo and Japanese voiced kana gain a sound mark, so those strings get longer.

Why does \b not work for Korean or Russian in JavaScript? In JavaScript a word character for \b is a letter from A to Z or a to z, a digit from 0 to 9, or an underscore. Korean, Cyrillic, Greek and Arabic letters are not word characters, so there is no boundary next to them, and /\bкот\b/ never matches "кот".

How do you make search accent-insensitive without breaking highlight positions? Fold the query and the text the same way for matching, then map the match back to the original string before slicing or highlighting. Folding cluster by cluster, a base character plus its marks, lets you record where each folded character came from.

Resources

  • Remove accents/diacritics in a string in JavaScript, Stack Overflow
  • String.prototype.normalize(), MDN
  • Word boundary assertion, MDN
  • UAX #15: Unicode Normalization Forms
  • Intl.Collator, MDN

title: MPF Mapping: A Myelin Readout From Routine Brain MRI
partialText:
AI-assistance disclosure: I drafted this article with AI assistance, then edited it and fact-checked every number against the paper (arXiv:2610.37213).

A self-supervised network turns T1w, T2w and FLAIR scans into macromolecular pool fraction maps, with public code and weights.

Most brain MRI archives are full of T1-weighted, T2-weighted and FLAIR scans, and almost none of them contain a quantitative myelin measurement. Getting one usually means adding a dedicated quantitative magnetization transfer (qMT) sequence, which costs scan time and only helps for patients scanned after you add it. Jelmer van Lune, Miha Fuderer, Oscar van der Heide, Matteo Maspero, Martin B. Schilder, Jan Willem Dankbaar, Stefano Mandija and Alessandro Sbrizzi at UMC Utrecht estimate the macromolecular pool fraction (MPF), a myelin-sensitive biomarker, straight from those three routine contrasts. The method is described in arXiv:2610.37213, and the PyTorch code and trained weights are on GitHub.

What MPF is, in one paragraph

In a two-pool model of brain tissue, part of the protons sit in free water and part are bound to macromolecules such as proteins and lipids. The bound protons relax far too fast to image directly, but they trade magnetization with the free water and change how fast the visible signal recovers. MPF is the fraction of protons in that bound pool. Myelin carries a lot of it, so MPF is lower where myelin is lost, and post-mortem work has tied reduced MPF to histological demyelination. MS studies use it for exactly that reason.

Why a clinic or viewer team should care

The input is the protocol most sites already run: a 3D T1w (spoiled gradient echo or MPRAGE), an axial 2D T2w turbo spin echo and a 3D FLAIR. The output is an MPF map, plus free-water T1, T2 and proton density maps, for every past and future session that has those scans. For a research archive that means retrospective myelin studies on thousands of patients without recalling anyone. For a viewer or PACS add-on, it is one more parametric overlay you can compute in the background and show next to FLAIR, the way the paper does in Figure 3.

Pipeline builders hit one catch: the physics model needs the acquisition parameters of each scan: TR, TE, TI, flip angle and the sequence-averaged RF power, B1rms. The authors pulled these from DICOM headers for the Utrecht data and from metadata files for the public set. B1rms has its own DICOM attribute (0018,1320), but anonymization tools and NIfTI conversions often drop it, so keep the original headers or a sidecar file.

How the method works

  1. A 2D U-Net reads all three contrasts. A shared encoder processes T1w, T2w and FLAIR slices separately, attention modules fuse the features at each level, and one decoder outputs four maps: free-water T1, free-water T2, proton density and MPF. The network has 9.06 million trainable parameters and works on 224 x 224 axial slices.
  2. The scanner settings steer the network. Each contrast comes with a nine-value vector (contrast type, log TR, log TE, sine of the flip angle, B1rms, inversion flag, log TI). A small MLP turns it into an embedding that drives adaptive instance normalization in the encoder, so the same weights read a Philips spoiled GRE and a Siemens MPRAGE differently.
  3. Training needs no reference maps. The predicted maps go through closed-form Bloch signal equations for each sequence type, with a magnetization transfer term that links apparent T1 to MPF and to the sequence’s RF power. The loss compares the synthesized T1w, T2w and FLAIR images with the acquired ones. Because free-water T1 and MPF can trade off against each other, a prior on white matter T1 and a soft lower bound on proton density keep the solution in a physical range.

Training ran for 20 epochs on 6,084 sessions and took about 12 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 4500 Ada GPU.

Data

The dataset combines 5,312 sessions from four Philips 3 T systems at UMC Utrecht with 2,393 sessions from a Siemens Magnetom Vida 3 T in the public MR-RATE dataset (Istanbul Medipol University), 7,705 sessions from 4,489 subjects in total. Subjects were split 80/5/15 into training, validation and test, so the test set holds 1,237 sessions. Preprocessing follows a standard neuro pipeline: dcm2niix, resampling to the T2w grid, rigid registration with ANTsPy, HD-BET skull stripping, N4 bias correction and SynthSeg tissue masks.

What the results show

White matter came out higher than gray matter in every vendor and protocol group, which is the expected order. In 70 MR-RATE test sessions with a report-derived demyelinating-disease label, lesions segmented with LST-AI had 35.6% lower MPF than normal-appearing white matter, in the range that dedicated qMT studies report for MS lesions. Four confirmed MS patients from Utrecht showed similar drops.

Archives mix protocols, so the authors tested consistency directly. They scanned one healthy volunteer twice in the same session, once with a spoiled GRE T1w protocol and once with MPRAGE, and the two MPF maps differed by 7.7% on average across brain tissue. Removing the acquisition conditioning roughly doubled that difference, to 15.3%.

Code, weights and license

The repository JelmervanL/MPF-mapping-from-conventional-MRI contains the training and inference code (Hydra configs, TorchIO data loading, the physics module) and a v1.0.0 release with the trained generator weights, a 36 MB latest_net_G.pth. Inputs are preprocessed NIfTI volumes plus one CSV row per session with the sequence parameters. The code and weights are under CC BY-NC 4.0, so commercial use needs a separate agreement with the authors. The paper itself is CC BY 4.0. The Utrecht data cannot be shared, but MR-RATE is available on Hugging Face under its own access terms.

Limits before you put it in front of a radiologist

  • Unseen sequence types break it. When the authors withheld spoiled GRE from training, the model put white matter MPF well below the in-domain values on those scans. Do not run the released weights on a T1w sequence family the model never saw without validating first.
  • Only 3 T, and a narrow protocol mix. All scans are 3 T, protocol variety is mostly in the T1w, and 3D T2w or 2D FLAIR were not represented.
  • No ground-truth qMT comparison. There were no paired qMT scans, so the evaluation rests on plausibility, lesion contrast and reproducibility. Gray matter and white matter are also closer together than in prospective qMT (a GM to WM ratio near 0.79 versus about 0.5).
  • Slice-wise and resampled. Everything is registered to the 2D T2w grid with 3 or 4 mm slices, so 3D detail from T1w and FLAIR is lost, and the network does not use neighbouring slices.
  • Soft labels. Disease labels come from radiology reports, the cross-protocol test used a single volunteer, and FLAIR lesions are not specific to demyelination.

Where it fits

We see two near-term uses. Research groups with large neuro archives can run it retrospectively to study myelin changes over years of routine follow-up, provided their T1w sequences resemble the training mix. Imaging software teams can treat it as a parametric map service: pull the three series and their headers from PACS, run the preprocessing chain, and push an MPF overlay back as a derived series for research review. The non-commercial license and the protocol limits both point to research use first.

Paper: van Lune J., Fuderer M., van der Heide O., Maspero M., Schilder M. B., Dankbaar J. W., Mandija S., Sbrizzi A. “Retrospective macromolecular pool fraction mapping from conventional clinical MRI: a physics-guided self-supervised deep learning framework.” arXiv:2610.37213, 2026. Featured image: Figures 3 and 6 of the paper (CC BY 4.0), cropped and resized only.
